clinicalPearls: A horizontally defined level below which sensory, motor, and autonomic function is impaired is the hallmark of a spinal cord lesion; the sensory level for pinprick/temperature is sought by moving the stimulus upward and is typically one to two segments below a unilateral cord lesion because second-order spinothalamic fibers ascend before crossing.

Because the cord segments do not align with the like-numbered vertebrae, lesion localization must account for offset: a sensory level at the umbilicus reflects T10 cord pathology, located adjacent to the seventh or eighth thoracic vertebral body.

Spinal shock can produce flaccid, areflexic paralysis acutely (lasting days, rarely weeks) and may be mistaken for extensive anterior horn cell damage or an acute polyneuropathy; hyperreflexia and spasticity supervene later, but persistent areflexic paralysis with a sensory level usually signifies necrosis across multiple cord segments.

Brown-Sequard (hemicord) syndrome combines ipsilateral weakness and loss of joint position/vibration sense with contralateral loss of pain and temperature one to two levels below the lesion; partial forms are more common than the full syndrome.

Central cord syndrome produces arm weakness out of proportion to leg weakness and a dissociated, suspended cape-distribution sensory loss (loss of pain/temperature with preserved touch, position, and vibration), classically from trauma, syringomyelia, or intrinsic cord tumor.

Anterior cord syndrome (anterior spinal artery territory) abolishes motor, pain/temperature, and autonomic function while strikingly sparing vibration and position sense carried in the posterior columns.

Sacral sparing favors an intramedullary process, reflecting the lamination of the spinothalamic tract with sacral fibers outermost; extramedullary lesions instead tend to cause prominent radicular pain and early sacral sensory loss.

Conus medullaris lesions cause symmetric saddle anesthesia (S3-S5), early prominent bladder/bowel dysfunction with lax anal tone and impotence, and relatively preserved strength; cauda equina lesions instead cause low back and radicular pain, asymmetric leg weakness/sensory loss, areflexia, and relative sparing of bowel/bladder.

A recent onset of persistent thoracic back pain that worsens with movement, coughing, or recumbency and awakens the patient at night should raise concern for vertebral metastasis, since the thoracic spine is uncommonly involved by spondylosis.

Spinal epidural abscess classically presents as the triad of midline back/neck pain, fever, and progressive limb weakness; once myelopathic signs appear progression can be rapid and irreversible, so early recognition is critical.

Spondylotic (degenerative cervical) myelopathy is the most common cause of myelopathy and gait disturbance in the elderly, suspected with progressive spastic paraparesis, foot/hand paresthesias, or wasting of intrinsic hand muscles.

Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency classically shows the combination of an absent ankle reflex (peripheral neuropathy) with an extensor plantar (Babinski) response, plus loss of vibration/position sense and a positive Romberg sign.
harrison.pathophysiology: The spinal cord packs nearly the entire motor output and sensory input of the trunk and limbs into a small cross-sectional area, so focal lesions produce disproportionately severe deficits (quadriplegia, paraplegia, sensory loss). Peripherally located white matter tracts carry ascending sensory (posterior columns for position/vibration, spinothalamic for pain/temperature) and descending motor (corticospinal) pathways, while gray matter contains neuronal cell bodies. The crossing pattern of the spinothalamic tract (decussating anterior to the central canal one to two segments above entry) and the same-side course of the posterior columns and corticospinal tracts generate the characteristic clinical syndromes. The cord is supplied by a single anterior spinal artery (anterior two-thirds) and paired posterior spinal arteries (posterior columns); a watershed zone in the upper thoracic cord makes T3-T4 vulnerable to infarction during hypotension or aortic cross-clamping. Disease mechanisms are grouped into compressive (tumor, abscess, hematoma, disk, spondylosis), vascular/ischemic, inflammatory/immune (MS, NMO, sarcoid, systemic autoimmune), infectious/postinfectious, metabolic/nutritional (B12, copper deficiency), developmental (syringomyelia, tethered cord), and degenerative/genetic categories.
additionalDifferentials: Acute polyneuropathy (e.g., Guillain-Barre) when ascending paresthesias begin in the feet -- bladder dysfunction and a sharp sensory level point instead to the cord
Compressive causes: epidural/intradural/intramedullary neoplasm, epidural abscess, epidural hematoma, herniated disk, cervical spondylosis, post-traumatic vertebral displacement
Vascular: anterior spinal artery infarction, dural arteriovenous fistula/AVM, hematomyelia, antiphospholipid syndrome and hypercoagulable states
Inflammatory/immune: multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica (AQP-4), anti-MOG and anti-GFAP disorders, sarcoidosis, SLE, Sjogren's, Behcet's, vasculitis, CLIPPERS, Erdheim-Chester
Metabolic/nutritional: vitamin B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration), folate deficiency, copper deficiency, nitrous oxide-induced myelopathy
Degenerative/genetic: hereditary spastic paraplegia, primary lateral sclerosis, adrenomyeloneuropathy
Developmental: syringomyelia, tethered cord syndrome, meningomyelocele
Cancer-related: radiation myelopathy, intrathecal methotrexate toxicity, paraneoplastic (anti-amphiphysin, CRMP5, Hu), checkpoint-inhibitor myelopathy
infectionMimics: Spinal epidural abscess (most commonly Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA)
Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott's disease) with epidural extension
Viral myelitis: herpes zoster, HSV-1 and HSV-2 (Elsberg syndrome with recurrent sacral neuritis), EBV, CMV, rabies, Zika
Poliomyelitis and polio-like acute flaccid paralysis (enterovirus A-71, D-68, West Nile and other flaviviruses)
Bacterial/mycobacterial myelitis: Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme), Listeria, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Treponema pallidum (syphilis, tabes dorsalis)
Retroviral myelopathy: HTLV-1 (tropical spastic paraparesis) and HIV vacuolar myelopathy
Parasitic: schistosomiasis (granulomatous), toxoplasmosis (especially in AIDS), cysticercosis
Postinfectious/postvaccinal myelitis (EBV, CMV, mycoplasma, influenza, measles, varicella, mumps, SARS-CoV-2)
nonInfectiousMimics: Multiple sclerosis and neuromyelitis optica presenting as acute or chronic myelitis
Anterior spinal artery infarction mimicking acute transverse myelitis
Dural arteriovenous fistula causing progressive myelopathy that can simulate MS or, with mixed upper/lower motor neuron signs, ALS
Foix-Alajouanine syndrome (subacute necrotic myelopathy from intramedullary vascular malformation)
Subacute combined degeneration and hypocupric myelopathy mimicking each other (B12 normal in copper deficiency)
Primary lateral sclerosis and hereditary spastic paraplegia presenting as slowly progressive spastic paraparesis
Spinal sarcoidosis mimicking tumor or NMO on imaging
Toxic myelopathies: lathyrism (BOAA in chickpeas) and Konzo (cyanogenic cassava)
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the spinal cord with and without gadolinium, centered on the suspected level, as the initial procedure to exclude compression; imaging the entire spine is often appropriate since up to 40% of patients with cord compression at one level have asymptomatic epidural metastases elsewhere

CSF analysis: cell count, protein, glucose, IgG index/synthesis rate, oligoclonal bands, VDRL, Gram/acid-fast/India ink stains, PCR for VZV/HSV/EBV/CMV/HHV-6/enterovirus/HIV, antibodies for HTLV-1, Borrelia, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia
Serum autoantibodies: anti-aquaporin-4, anti-MOG, anti-GFAP for NMO and related disorders
Serum vitamin B12 with macrocytic indices, and confirmatory elevated homocysteine and methylmalonic acid; serum copper and ceruloplasmin for hypocupric myelopathy

Workup for systemic autoimmune disease: ESR, ANA, dsDNA, rheumatoid factor, anti-SSA/SSB, complement, antiphospholipid/anticardiolipin antibodies, pANCA; serum/CSF ACE, calcium, chest CT, gallium scan for sarcoid
Vascular evaluation: MR/CT angiography and selective spinal angiography (definitive) for suspected AVM or dural fistula; CT myelogram when MRI unavailable
Paraneoplastic antibody panel (amphiphysin, CRMP5, Hu) when malignancy suspected
Diffusion-weighted MRI and recognition of cord-infarction signs (anterior 'pencil-like' T2 signal, 'owl's eyes' axial hyperintensities, adjacent vertebral body infarction)
redFlags: Neck or back pain with progressive limb weakness, bladder disturbance, or a sensory level -- treatable cord compression must be excluded urgently with MRI
Fever with spinal pain and progressive weakness suggesting epidural abscess
New persistent thoracic back pain in a patient with known or suspected malignancy
Hyperextension neck injury in a patient with degenerative cervical stenosis (acute spondylotic myelopathy / central cord syndrome)
Autonomic dysreflexia (paroxysmal hypertension, headache, flushing, diaphoresis, bradycardia) from a noxious stimulus below a lesion at or above T6
Quadriplegic fever and loss of normal somatic/visceral pain signaling masking infection, thrombophlebitis, or intra-abdominal pathology in chronic cord injury
Diaphragmatic weakness with upper cervical lesions
harrison.prognosis: Many spinal cord diseases are reversible if recognized and treated early, making them among the most critical neurologic emergencies. For neoplastic compression, ambulatory status at presentation predicts a good outcome; motor deficits established for more than 12 hours rarely improve, and beyond 48 hours the prognosis for substantial motor recovery is poor. With prompt diagnosis and treatment of spinal epidural abscess, up to two-thirds of patients achieve significant recovery, but fixed deficits more than several days old are unlikely to reverse. After cord infarction, severe motor weakness and persistent areflexia predict poor recovery, though more than half of patients in one series regained some ambulation. The prospects for recovery from an acute destructive lesion fade after about 6 months, and there are currently no effective means to repair injured cord tissue. Even complete high cervical lesions can be compatible with a productive life; ultimate disability is determined chiefly by lesion level and whether the deficit is complete or incomplete.
pitfalls: Mistaking spinal shock (acute flaccid areflexic paralysis) for a polyneuropathy or for diffuse anterior horn cell disease
Attributing ascending foot paresthesias to peripheral neuropathy and overlooking bladder dysfunction and a sensory level indicating a cord origin
Relying on plain radiographs or radionuclide bone scans, which miss 15-20% of metastatic vertebral lesions and fail to detect paravertebral masses reaching the epidural space through the foramina
Gadolinium contrast can deceptively 'normalize' the appearance of a vertebral metastasis on T1 imaging by raising its signal to that of normal marrow
Failing to image the entire spine when cord compression is found at one level, missing clinically silent additional metastases
Assuming MRI is sensitive for cord infarction early -- it may be normal in the first day
Interpreting HTLV-1 seropositivity alone as proof of causation for a myelopathy in endemic areas
Lumbar puncture in severe thrombocytopenia/coagulopathy (risk of epidural hematoma) or through tissue overlying an epidural abscess (risk of seeding meningitis) -- a high cervical tap may be safer
Overlooking copper deficiency (with normal B12) as a cause of a subacute-combined-degeneration-like myelopathy, particularly after bariatric surgery or with excess zinc intake
harrison.severityClassification: Functional outcome after complete cord lesions is stratified by level (Harrison Table 453-4): high quadriplegia (C1-C4) -- dependent on others, requires respiratory support, motorized wheelchair; low quadriplegia (C5-C8) -- partially independent with adaptive equipment, may use a manual wheelchair and drive with adaptations; paraplegia (below T1) -- independent in self-care and transfers, ambulates short distances with aids. Lesions are also characterized clinically as complete versus incomplete, and intramedullary versus extramedullary (and extradural versus intradural, the former generally malignant and the latter benign).
